title: The Invention of the Traffic Light
summary: The story of how police officers directing traffic by hand were replaced by electric traffic lights, which added a yellow caution light and made streets safer everywhere.
poll: The invention of the three-color traffic light did more to make city streets safe than any traffic rule written on paper.

versions.title: The Invention of the Traffic Light
versions.text:
Long ago, streets were busy and messy. Horses and carts moved at once. People walked too. There were no rules. Crashes happened a lot.

At first, a man stood at the corner. He was a police officer. He used his hands. He told traffic to stop. He told traffic to go.

A man named Lester Wire had an idea. He made a box. It had two lights. One light was red. One light was green. Red meant stop. Green meant go.

Soon, cities put up lights like this. A worker sat in a small room. The worker turned the lights on and off.

Later, a man in Detroit added one more light. It was yellow. Yellow meant go slow. Now there were three lights.

These lights spread to many cities. They made streets much safer. Drivers knew just what to do.

Red instructed drivers to stop immediately, while green indicated that it was safe to proceed, and historians consider his invention one of the earliest electric traffic signals built anywhere in the world.

Soon afterward, other rapidly growing cities began installing signals modeled closely on Wire's original design, though initially a human operator still had to sit inside a small booth near the intersection, controlling the lights entirely by hand throughout the working day, switching between colors as needed and watching the traffic build up below.

In 1920, a police officer working in Detroit added one more essential light to this basic signal: a yellow caution light, which warned drivers to slow down and proceed carefully before the signal finally changed to red. With this single addition, every modern traffic signal now operated as a fully automatic system with three distinct, standardized colors: red, yellow, and green, a combination still used almost everywhere today.

These reliable three-light signals quickly spread to cities across the entire country, and eventually around the world, making busy intersections dramatically safer for drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians attempting to cross each day without any direct assistance from a human officer standing in the street.

Horses, carts, bicycles, and pedestrians all competed for the same narrow space at once, with no consistent rules for anyone involved to follow, regardless of how experienced a traveler happened to be. He used his arms as signals, directing traffic to stop with one motion and proceed with another, but this exhausting, human-controlled system meant a single officer could not realistically control more than one intersection at any given time, no matter how skilled he was.

In 1912, a police officer named Lester Wire, working in Salt Lake City, devised a genuinely clever solution to this persistent, citywide problem that had frustrated officers for years. He built a simple wooden device fitted with two colored lights, one red and one green, powered by electricity rather than relying on hand signals alone. Soon afterward, other rapidly growing cities began installing signals modeled closely on Wire's original design, though initially a human operator still had to sit inside a small booth near the intersection, controlling the lights entirely by hand throughout the entire working day, switching between colors as the traffic required.

In 1920, a police officer working in Detroit added one more essential light to this basic signal: a yellow caution light, which warned drivers to slow down and proceed carefully before the signal finally changed to red, giving them time to react. With this single addition, every modern traffic signal now operated as a fully automatic system with three distinct, standardized colors: red, yellow, and green.

These reliable three-light signals quickly spread to cities across the entire country, and eventually around the world, making busy intersections dramatically safer for drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians attempting to cross each day without any direct assistance from a human officer standing in the street, and permanently changing how traffic would be managed from then on into the future.

MID.prompt: Explain how traffic signals changed from a police officer using hand signals to an electric light with three colors.
checklist: Describe how a police officer controlled traffic before signals.
Explain what Lester Wire and the Detroit officer each added.
Use at least one key word, like signal, officer, or caution.
MID.modelAnswer: At first, a police officer stood at a corner and used hand signals to control traffic, which tired him out and only worked for one street at a time. In 1912, officer Lester Wire built an electric box with red and green lights, so cars knew when to stop and go without a person signaling. In 1920, a police officer in Detroit added a yellow caution light, warning drivers to slow down before the light turned red. These changes made signals automatic and much easier for everyone to understand.

HIGH.modelAnswer: The traffic light became both automatic and standardized because, once Lester Wire's electric red-and-green design was improved with a yellow caution light in Detroit in 1920, every modern signal used the same three colors with the same meanings everywhere. This replaced the exhausting, inconsistent system of a single police officer manually directing one intersection at a time. Because the lights worked by themselves, they could manage many intersections at once, freeing officers for other duties and letting drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians cross busy streets safely without needing a person to guide them.
